claim: The study assembled a large panel of 696 Escherichia coli strains that were genotyped.
source: Here we have assembled a large panel of 696 Escherichia coli strains, which we have genotyped and measured their phenotypic profile across 214 growth conditions.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract with specific numbers of strains and conditions tested.

claim: The study measured phenotypic profiles of the E. coli strains across 214 growth conditions.
source: Here we have assembled a large panel of 696 Escherichia coli strains, which we have genotyped and measured their phenotypic profile across 214 growth conditions.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract with specific number of conditions.

claim: The study integrated variant effect predictors to derive gene-level probabilities of loss of function for every gene across all strains.
source: We integrated variant effect predictors to derive gene-level probabilities of loss of function for every gene across all strains.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the computational methodology.

claim: The study combined gene-level loss of function probabilities with information on conditional gene essentiality in the reference K-12 strain to compute growth defects.
source: Finally, we combined these probabilities with information on conditional gene essentiality in the reference K-12 strain to compute the growth defects of each strain.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the predictive model approach.

claim: The predictive model could reliably predict growth defects in up to 38% of tested conditions.
source: Not only could we reliably predict these defects in up to 38% of tested conditions, but we could also directly identify the causal variants that were validated through complementation assays.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract with specific percentage of successful predictions.

claim: Causal variants identified by the model were validated through complementation assays.
source: Not only could we reliably predict these defects in up to 38% of tested conditions, but we could also directly identify the causal variants that were validated through complementation assays.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing experimental validation.

claim: GWAS studies often fall short in pinpointing causal variants due to lack of power to resolve variants in linkage disequilibrium.
source: While such approaches are powerful in elucidating trait heritability and disease associations (Yang et al., 2010; Welter et al., 2014), they often fall short in pinpointing causal variants, either due to lack of power to resolve variants in linkage disequilibrium (Edwards et al., 2013) or for the dispersion of weak association signals across a large number of regions across the genome (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2013.

claim: GWAS studies often fall short in pinpointing causal variants due to dispersion of weak association signals across a large number of regions across the genome.
source: While such approaches are powerful in elucidating trait heritability and disease associations (Yang et al., 2010; Welter et al., 2014), they often fall short in pinpointing causal variants, either due to lack of power to resolve variants in linkage disequilibrium (Edwards et al., 2013) or for the dispersion of weak association signals across a large number of regions across the genome (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyle et al., 2017.

claim: GWAS studies are unable to assess the impact of previously unseen or rare variants.
source: Furthermore, by definition GWAS studies are unable to assess the impact of previously unseen or rare variants, which can often have a large effect on phenotype (Bodmer and Bonilla, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodmer and Bonilla, 2008.

claim: Rare variants can often have a large effect on phenotype.
source: Furthermore, by definition GWAS studies are unable to assess the impact of previously unseen or rare variants, which can often have a large effect on phenotype (Bodmer and Bonilla, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodmer and Bonilla, 2008.

claim: Genome-wide knock-out libraries of different organisms have been profiled across multiple growth conditions.
source: Such knowledge is now readily available by chemical genetics approaches, in which genome-wide knock-out (KO) libraries of different organisms are profiled across multiple growth conditions (Kamath et al., 2003; Dietzl et al., 2007; Hillenmeyer et al., 2008; Nichols et al., 2011; Price et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies in different organisms.

claim: The impact of variants on gene function can be reliably inferred using different computational approaches.
source: The impact of variants on gene function can be reliably inferred using different computational approaches (Thusberg et al., 2011; Kulshreshtha et al., 2016), which can offer mechanistic insights into how such variants impact on a protein's structure and function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Thusberg et al., 2011 and Kulshreshtha et al., 2016.

claim: Combining variant effect predictors with gene conditional essentiality has been previously tested with some success in Saccharomyces cerevisiae on 15 individuals and 20 conditions.
source: Combining variant effector predictors with gene conditional essentiality has been previously tested with some success in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, but only on a limited number of individuals and conditions (15 and 20, respectively, Jelier et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jelier et al., 2011 with specific numbers provided.

claim: Diversity within the same bacterial species can result in two individuals differing by as much as half of their genomic content.
source: In contrast to eukaryotes, diversity within the same bacterial species can result in two individuals differing by as much as half of their genomic content.
evidence: General statement about bacterial diversity based on established knowledge.

claim: Escherichia coli is one of the most studied organisms to date.
source: Escherichia coli is not only one of the most studied organisms to date (Blount, 2015), but also one of the most genetically diverse bacterial species (Lukjancenko et al., 2010; Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blount, 2015.

claim: Escherichia coli is one of the most genetically diverse bacterial species.
source: Escherichia coli is not only one of the most studied organisms to date (Blount, 2015), but also one of the most genetically diverse bacterial species (Lukjancenko et al., 2010; Tenaillon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lukjancenko et al., 2010 and Tenaillon et al., 2010.

claim: Gene conditional essentiality has been heavily profiled for the reference E. coli strain K-12.
source: Since gene conditional essentiality has been heavily profiled for the reference E. coli strain (K-12, Nichols et al., 2011; Price et al., 2016), here we set out to systematically test the applicability of such genotype-to-phenotype predictive models for this species.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nichols et al., 2011 and Price et al., 2016.

source: Resulting assembled contigs were annotated for coding genes, ribosomal RNAs and tRNAs using Prokka (Seemann, 2014) version 1.11.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: SNPs were called through whole genome alignment using ParSNP version 1.2.
source: Due to the variability in sequencing technologies or lack of the original reads for the already sequenced strains in the collection (N = 373), SNPs were called through a whole genome alignment between each strain and the genome of the reference individual (Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655, RefSeq accession: NC_000913.3, strain collection identifier NT12001), using ParSNP (Treangen et al., 2014) version 1.2.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: The reference strain is Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655 (RefSeq accession: NC_000913.3).
source: Due to the variability in sequencing technologies or lack of the original reads for the already sequenced strains in the collection (N = 373), SNPs were called through a whole genome alignment between each strain and the genome of the reference individual (Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655, RefSeq accession: NC_000913.3, strain collection identifier NT12001), using ParSNP (Treangen et al., 2014) version 1.2.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods.

claim: Functional impact of nonsynonymous substitutions was computed using SIFT version 5.1.1.
source: Functional impact of nonsynonymous substitutions has been computed using SIFT (Ng and Henikoff, 2001) version 5.1.1, using uniref50 as a sequence search database.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: Structural impact of nonsynonymous substitutions was computed using FoldX version 4.
source: Structural impact of nonsynonymous substitutions has been computed using FoldX (Guerois et al., 2002) version 4; both 3-D structures present in the PDB database and homology models were used.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: Homology models were created using ModPipe version 2.2.0.
source: Homology models were created using ModPipe (Pieper et al., 2014) version 2.2.0.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: Mutations with known impact on the reference individual were downloaded from Uniprot (N = 3673).
source: Mutations with known impact on the reference individual have been downloaded from Uniprot (UniProt Consortium, 2015, N = 3673) and used to derive such conversion; since only 580 mutations are reported to have a neutral impact, we added all observed nonsynonymous variants affecting known essential genes (as reported in the OGEE database, Chen et al., 2017) to the list of tolerated mutations.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation and specific number.

claim: Only 580 mutations from Uniprot are reported to have a neutral impact.
source: Mutations with known impact on the reference individual have been downloaded from Uniprot (UniProt Consortium, 2015, N = 3673) and used to derive such conversion; since only 580 mutations are reported to have a neutral impact, we added all observed nonsynonymous variants affecting known essential genes (as reported in the OGEE database, Chen et al., 2017) to the list of tolerated mutations.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with specific number.

claim: Variants with relatively high frequency (>=10%) in the strains collection were not considered in the disruption score calculation.
source: Variants with relatively high frequency (>=10%) in the strains collection were not considered, as well as those reference genes that are absent in a significant number of strains (>=10%), as we reasoned that they are unlikely to be deleterious given their high observed frequency.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with specific threshold.

claim: Reference genes that are absent in a significant number of strains (>=10%) were not considered in the disruption score calculation.
source: Variants with relatively high frequency (>=10%) in the strains collection were not considered, as well as those reference genes that are absent in a significant number of strains (>=10%), as we reasoned that they are unlikely to be deleterious given their high observed frequency.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with specific threshold.

claim: The strain collection was plated in three solid agar plates, each containing 1536 single colonies.
source: The strain collection was plated in three solid agar plates, each one containing 1536 single colonies, so that each strain was plated at least four times in each plate, each time with different neighboring strains.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods.

claim: Each strain was plated at least four times in each plate with different neighboring strains.
source: The strain collection was plated in three solid agar plates, each one containing 1536 single colonies, so that each strain was plated at least four times in each plate, each time with different neighboring strains.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods.

claim: Three replicates were prepared for each condition.
source: For each condition we prepared three replicates (each one using a different source plate to reduce batch effects) with the concentrations indicated in Supplementary file 2 and the addition of the Cosmos dye (CAS number 573-58-0) and Coomasie brilliant blue R-250 (CAS number 6104-59-2).
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods.

claim: Colony parameters were extracted using Iris version 0.9.4.71.
source: A series of colony parameters were extracted from each photograph, using Iris (Kritikos et al., 2017) version 0.9.4.71: colony size, opacity, roundness and color intensity.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: The EMAP algorithm was used to derive S-scores with default parameters.
source: The final colony sizes were used as an input for the EMAP algorithm (Collins et al., 2006), with default parameters, in order to derive an S-score, which informs on the deviation of each strain from the expected growth in each condition.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods with citation.

claim: New genomic sequences have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) with accession number PRJEB20550.
source: New genomic sequences have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) with accession number PRJEB20550.
evidence: Directly stated in Materials and methods.

claim: The correlation between replicates of the complementation experiment was high (Pearson's r: 0.94).
source: Overall, we observed a high correlation between replicates of this experiment (Pearson's r: 0.94, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated with specific correlation value and reference to figure.

claim: The clustering of conditions based on phenotypic profiles was consistent with the conditions macro-categories.
source: Clustering of conditions based on phenotypic profiles across all strains was consistent with the conditions macro-categories (e.g. stresses versus nutrient sources) and with the number of sensitive strains (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The correlation of phenotypic profiles clustered drugs with same mode of action.
source: The correlation of phenotypic profiles also clustered drugs with same mode of action (MoA), as shown by comparing the clusters' purity against those of random clusters (Figure 1D).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Most variants across these strains have a neutral impact on their phenotypes.
source: This finding reinforces the idea that most variants across these strains have a neutral impact on their phenotypes.
evidence: Inference from the lack of correlation between genetic and phenotypic distance.

claim: Few DNA variants are sufficient to cause clear phenotypic differences.
source: These results clearly underline that simple metrics of phylogenetic similarity are not predictive of differences in phenotype. Instead, few DNA variants are sufficient to cause clear phenotypic differences, indicating the importance of statistical or predictive strategies to prioritize those variants.
evidence: Directly stated based on observations from LTEE strains.

claim: The effect of the loss of function of a gene is assumed to be independent of the genetic background.
source: We reasoned that it would also test the limits of the underlying assumption of this model, which is that the effect of the loss of function of a gene is independent of the genetic background (Dowell et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated as an assumption of the model with citation.

claim: The set of conditionally essential genes has diverged substantially across strains.
source: Since our predictions did not apply equally well for all conditions, we conclude that the set of conditionally essential genes has diverged substantially across strains.
evidence: Conclusion based on variable prediction accuracy across conditions.
